Extract and Display Fit Statistics for OLS Models from SCF Data

Source: R/scf_fit_ols.R
scf_fit_ols.Rd

scf_fit_ols() extracts and summarizes model fit statistics from an OLS regression estimated on multiply-imputed Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) data using scf_ols(). It is designed to provide a concise overview of model performance by reporting the average R-squared and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) across imputations.

scf_fit_ols(model)

Arguments

model

A model object returned by scf_ols(). This object must be a data.frame with attributes r.squared, AIC, and models, all of which are automatically returned by the scf_ols() function.

Value

A named list containing:

r.squared

The average R-squared value across all implicates

AIC

The average AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) across all implicates

imputations

The number of implicates (usually 5)

The function also prints a summary of these statistics to the console.

Details

This function is useful when comparing alternative model specifications or evaluating the overall goodness-of-fit of a regression estimated using multiply-imputed data. It helps assess how well a given model explains the variation in net worth (or other outcome variables) in the SCF microdata.

In multiply-imputed SCF data, each model is fit on multiple versions of the data, called "implicates", that reflect uncertainty from missing-data imputation. Traditional model diagnostics like R-squared and AIC do not pool across implicates using Rubin’s Rules, because they are not parameters. Instead, the conventional practice is to average these diagnostics across the fitted models.

This function follows that convention by averaging R-squared and AIC values across the implicates estimated within scf_ols(). It assumes that model output includes a models attribute (a list of lm() objects), as well as computed attributes r.squared and AIC.

Workflow Integration

scf_fit_ols() is meant to complement scf_ols() and supports workflows involving model specification, diagnostics, and comparison across alternative regressions.

See also

scf_ols() for regression model estimation, scf_glm() for generalized linear models, scf_update() to transform or create variables in SCF data.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Load and prepare SCF data
scf2022 <- scf_load(2022)
scf2022 <- scf_update(scf2022, ~log_nw := log(networth + 1))

# Estimate OLS model on log net worth
model <- scf_ols(scf2022, log_nw ~ age + income + factor(edcl))

# View fit statistics
scf_fit_ols(model)
} # }
